name: New York, 1925
basis: Real New York City as it stood in 1925, written from general historical knowledge: neighborhoods, institutions, theaters, clubs, restaurants and ballparks that existed that year, with Prohibition, segregation and the immigrant city described as they were. No fictional characters or later places.
summary: New York in 1925: the biggest city in America and still growing, with skyscrapers going up in Midtown, subways pushing out to the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens, speakeasies behind every other door under Prohibition, Broadway and the Ziegfeld Follies, the Harlem Renaissance uptown and crowded immigrant neighborhoods downtown.

curated-2026-10.title: New York in 1925, written for Prospero Dungeon
curated-2026-10.note: Jazz Age New York from general historical knowledge: neighborhoods, institutions, theaters, nightclubs, restaurants, ballparks and employers that existed in 1925, at approximate real coordinates. Treat it as a snapshot for fiction, not a directory: clubs opened, were padlocked by Prohibition agents and reopened under new names all the time. Rents are rounded monthly figures in 1925 dollars for a furnished room, a two-room flat and a four-room flat. Prices and the day wage are rounded typical figures. Climate figures are rounded New York averages of the period.

neighborhoods.name: Harlem
neighborhoods.summary: The capital of Black America and the heart of the Harlem Renaissance: writers, artists and musicians, churches and lodges, cabarets on Lenox and Seventh Avenues, and rents set high for Black tenants, which the rent party helps pay.

neighborhoods.name: Hamilton Heights and Sugar Hill
neighborhoods.summary: Handsome row houses and apartment houses on the heights above Harlem around City College, where Black doctors, lawyers and musicians are beginning to move in, with the Polo Grounds below the bluff.

neighborhoods.name: San Juan Hill
neighborhoods.summary: Crowded tenement blocks in the West Sixties between Amsterdam Avenue and the river, the city's largest Black neighborhood before Harlem, with dance halls, churches and the New York Central freight yards.

neighborhoods.name: Upper West Side and Morningside Heights
neighborhoods.summary: Big apartment houses and brownstones between Central Park and Riverside Drive, with the Natural History Museum, Columbia University on the heights and many Jewish families who have moved up from downtown.

neighborhoods.name: Yorkville and the Upper East Side
neighborhoods.summary: German, Hungarian and Czech Yorkville around East 86th Street, with its dance halls, bakeries and gymnastic societies, below the mansions of Fifth Avenue's Millionaires' Row and the Metropolitan Museum.

neighborhoods.name: Midtown and Fifth Avenue
neighborhoods.summary: Fifth Avenue shops and churches, the Public Library, Grand Central Terminal and new office towers going up around them, with hotels, clubs and the Algonquin crowd on the side streets.

neighborhoods.name: Times Square and the Theater District
neighborhoods.summary: The electric signs of the Great White Way, some seventy legitimate theaters, vaudeville and movie palaces, dance halls, all-night restaurants and speakeasies in the side streets of the West Forties.

neighborhoods.name: Herald Square and the Garment District
neighborhoods.summary: Macy's and Gimbels at Herald Square, Pennsylvania Station, the new garment lofts of Seventh Avenue full of cutters and pressers, and Tin Pan Alley's song publishers a few blocks south.

neighborhoods.name: Hell's Kitchen
neighborhoods.summary: Irish tenement blocks on the West Side between Eighth Avenue and the river, with freight trains in the street, the Ninth Avenue market under the El, gangs, gyms and the new Madison Square Garden.

neighborhoods.name: Chelsea
neighborhoods.summary: West Side blocks of row houses and tenements by the Hudson piers where the big ocean liners dock, with the National Biscuit Company bakery, the meat market on Gansevoort Street and the old Hotel Chelsea.

neighborhoods.name: Greenwich Village
neighborhoods.summary: Crooked old streets of bohemians, little theaters, tea rooms and hidden speakeasies around Washington Square, beside Italian families on Bleecker Street and NYU on the square.

neighborhoods.name: Union Square and Gramercy
neighborhoods.summary: Soapbox speakers and cut-price stores on Union Square, Tammany Hall on Fourteenth Street, Gramercy Park's locked garden and the Flatiron Building on Madison Square, with Cooper Union down at Astor Place.

neighborhoods.name: Lower East Side
neighborhoods.summary: The most crowded neighborhood in America: Jewish tenements, pushcart markets on Orchard and Hester Streets, synagogues, settlement houses, Yiddish theaters on Second Avenue and delicatessens.

neighborhoods.name: Little Italy
neighborhoods.summary: Mulberry Street and its neighbors, packed with families from Naples and Sicily: pushcarts, pastry shops, social clubs, wine cellars and the saints' feasts of summer.

neighborhoods.name: Chinatown and the Bowery
neighborhoods.summary: A few crooked blocks of Mott, Pell and Doyers Streets, mostly men kept apart from their families by the exclusion laws, beside the Bowery's flophouses, missions and pawnshops under the Third Avenue El.

neighborhoods.name: City Hall and Park Row
neighborhoods.summary: City Hall and its park, the Woolworth Building, the newspapers of Park Row, the courts and the Tombs, with the Brooklyn Bridge rising out of it and what is left of the old Five Points nearby.

neighborhoods.name: Wall Street and the Battery
neighborhoods.summary: Banks, brokers and the Stock Exchange in narrow canyons at the tip of Manhattan, crowded with clerks and runners by day, with Battery Park, the Aquarium and the ferries to Ellis Island, the Statue and Staten Island.

neighborhoods.name: Brooklyn Heights and Downtown Brooklyn
neighborhoods.summary: Old brownstone streets on the bluff over the harbor, Borough Hall, the department stores of Fulton Street and, a little east, the Brooklyn Navy Yard.

neighborhoods.name: Williamsburg and Greenpoint
neighborhoods.summary: Factory and waterfront Brooklyn by the Williamsburg Bridge: sugar refineries, Jewish families who came over the bridge from the Lower East Side, Italian blocks and Polish Greenpoint to the north.

neighborhoods.name: Flatbush and Prospect Park
neighborhoods.summary: Leafy Brooklyn of frame houses and new apartment houses around Prospect Park, the Botanic Garden and Ebbets Field, where the Robins play.

neighborhoods.name: Coney Island
neighborhoods.summary: The Nickel Empire at the end of the subway: the new boardwalk, the beach, Luna Park and Steeplechase, hot dogs and bathhouses, packed on summer Sundays and quiet in winter.

neighborhoods.name: The Bronx and the Grand Concourse
neighborhoods.summary: New apartment houses with elevators going up along the Grand Concourse for families moving out of Manhattan, Yankee Stadium at 161st Street, the Zoo and the Botanical Garden, and Italian Belmont around Arthur Avenue.

neighborhoods.name: Astoria and Long Island City
neighborhoods.summary: Queens across the East River: factories and rail yards in Long Island City, German, Italian and Irish blocks in Astoria, the Steinway piano works and the Famous Players-Lasky movie studio.

neighborhoods.name: Hoboken, New Jersey
neighborhoods.summary: A mile-square German and Italian river town across the Hudson, with the Lackawanna terminal, transatlantic piers, Stevens Institute and a reputation for easygoing saloons, reached by ferry or the Hudson tubes.

transit.name: IRT subway
transit.summary: The Interborough Rapid Transit's subway: the Broadway-Seventh Avenue line up the West Side and the Lexington Avenue line up the East Side, with branches into the Bronx and Brooklyn. A nickel a ride.

transit.name: BMT subway
transit.summary: The Brooklyn-Manhattan Transit's Broadway line under Manhattan, the lines out to Coney Island and Astoria, and the new Fourteenth Street line to Williamsburg. A nickel.

transit.name: Third and Second Avenue Els
transit.summary: Steel elevated railways over the Bowery, Second and Third Avenues from South Ferry to the Bronx, noisy and dark underneath but quick, for a nickel.

transit.name: Sixth and Ninth Avenue Els
transit.summary: Elevated lines up the West Side over Sixth Avenue, Ninth Avenue and Columbus Avenue to Harlem and the Polo Grounds.

transit.name: Hudson tubes
transit.summary: The Hudson and Manhattan Railroad under the river from Hoboken and Jersey City to Hudson Terminal downtown and up Sixth Avenue to 33rd Street.

transit.name: Streetcars
transit.summary: Electric trolleys on the crosstown streets and up Broadway, and a web of lines across Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens and Hoboken. Brooklynites dodging them gave the ball club its nickname.

transit.name: Fifth Avenue Coach
transit.summary: Double-decker motor buses on Fifth Avenue and Riverside Drive, a dime a ride, with open tops for the view in summer.

transit.name: Harbor ferries
transit.summary: Ferries from the Battery to Staten Island, Ellis Island and the Statue, and across the Hudson from Barclay, Christopher and 23rd Streets to Hoboken.

transit.name: Pennsylvania Railroad
transit.summary: Trains from Pennsylvania Station under the Hudson to Newark, Philadelphia and points west, and under the East River on the Long Island Rail Road.

transit.name: New York Central
transit.summary: Trains from Grand Central Terminal up the Hudson and to Westchester, with a stop at 125th Street in Harlem.

transit.name: Taxicabs
transit.summary: Yellow and Checker cabs cruising Manhattan, about twenty cents for the first quarter mile; private motorcars crowd Fifth Avenue too.

transit.name: Walking
transit.summary: Most New Yorkers walk everywhere they can, and a nickel saved on a short ride is a nickel for coffee.

places.name: The Cotton Club
places.summary: Owney Madden's nightclub at Lenox Avenue and 142nd Street: Black dancers and a hot band in elaborate revues, a whites-only audience, steep prices and liquor served under the noses of the law.

places.name: Connie's Inn
places.summary: Connie and George Immerman's basement club on Seventh Avenue at 131st Street, with revues and a hot band, and, like the Cotton Club, white customers only.

places.name: Small's Paradise
places.summary: Ed Smalls's big basement cabaret at Seventh Avenue and 135th Street, opened in the fall of 1925: Black-owned, open to everyone, with waiters who dance the Charleston carrying trays.

places.name: Leroy's
places.summary: Leroy Wilkins's cabaret at Fifth Avenue and 135th Street, one of Harlem's oldest, where the stride pianists cut each other late at night and the crowd is from the neighborhood.

places.name: Lafayette Theatre
places.summary: The big theater on Seventh Avenue at 132nd Street, home of the Lafayette Players stock company and of revues, with the "Tree of Hope" outside where performers wait for work.

places.name: 135th Street Branch Library
places.summary: The Public Library's Harlem branch, where the new Division of Negro Literature, History and Prints opened in 1925 and young writers meet for readings.

places.name: Abyssinian Baptist Church
places.summary: One of the largest Protestant congregations in the country, in its new Gothic church on West 138th Street since 1923, led by the Reverend Adam Clayton Powell Sr.

places.name: Strivers' Row
places.summary: The elegant row houses of West 138th and 139th Streets, home to Harlem's doctors, lawyers and successful musicians, with signs on the gates asking people to walk their horses.

places.name: Liberty Hall
places.summary: The meeting hall of Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association on West 138th Street, still full on meeting nights though Garvey himself went to federal prison in Atlanta in February 1925.

places.name: Lenox Avenue lunchrooms
places.summary: Counters and family restaurants along Lenox Avenue serving Southern cooking: fried chicken, pork chops, greens, biscuits and sweet potato pie, till late for the musicians.

places.name: The Polo Grounds
places.summary: The horseshoe-shaped home of John McGraw's New York Giants under Coogan's Bluff at 155th Street, where people without tickets watch from the bluff for free.

places.name: Jumel Mansion
places.summary: The colonial house on the heights at 160th Street where Washington had his headquarters in 1776, kept as a museum by patriotic societies.

places.name: St. Nicholas Park
places.summary: A steep green park climbing from Harlem up to City College, with long stone stairways and views east over the rooftops.

places.name: Amsterdam Avenue lunchroom
places.summary: A steam-table lunchroom near City College where students and clerks get soup, a hot sandwich and pie for a quarter or two.

places.name: Convent Avenue drugstore soda fountain
places.summary: A marble-counter soda fountain in a corner drugstore: egg creams, ice cream sodas, coffee and gossip.

places.name: The Jungles Casino
places.summary: A rough basement dance hall on West 62nd Street where dockworkers from the Carolinas dance to James P. Johnson's stride piano, and where people say the Charleston took shape.

places.name: St. Cyprian's Chapel
places.summary: An Episcopal chapel and mission on West 63rd Street serving the neighborhood's Black families with services, a gym and a day nursery.

places.name: Columbus Circle
places.summary: The traffic circle at the corner of Central Park with Columbus on his column and the Maine monument, where soapbox speakers draw crowds on summer evenings.

places.name: West 61st Street speakeasy
places.summary: A back room behind a tailor's front on West 61st Street pouring gin and needle beer to dockworkers and musicians.

places.name: Amsterdam Avenue fish fry
places.summary: Fried porgies, whiting and cornbread from a storefront kitchen, wrapped in newspaper on Friday nights.

places.name: Central Park
places.summary: Olmsted and Vaux's great park: the Mall and its bandstand, rowboats on the Lake, the Sheep Meadow with real sheep, skating when the ponds freeze and carriage drives.

places.name: American Museum of Natural History
places.summary: The great museum on Central Park West, with dinosaur skeletons, Roy Chapman Andrews's dinosaur eggs from the Gobi and halls of animals in painted settings.

places.name: Grant's Tomb and Riverside Drive
places.summary: The granite tomb of General Grant high over the Hudson, at the end of a long promenade along Riverside Drive.

places.name: Cathedral of St. John the Divine
places.summary: The vast Episcopal cathedral on Morningside Heights, half built, with a citywide campaign under way in 1925 to raise money for its nave.

places.name: Childs on upper Broadway
places.summary: A white-tiled Childs restaurant with a cook flipping wheatcakes in the window, clean, cheap and open early and late.

places.name: Upper Broadway delicatessen
places.summary: A busy delicatessen for corned beef, pastrami, pickles and celery tonic, crowded after the movie houses let out.

places.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
places.summary: The great art museum on Fifth Avenue at 82nd Street, with Egyptian tombs, armor, Old Masters and a new American Wing opened in 1924.

places.name: Central Park Menagerie
places.summary: The free menagerie behind the old Arsenal at Fifth Avenue and 64th Street, with lions, bears, monkeys and seals, popular with families on Sundays.

places.name: Yorkville Casino
places.summary: A big hall on East 86th Street for German dances, club balls, concerts, boxing and union meetings.

places.name: New York Turn Verein
places.summary: The German gymnastic society's building on Lexington Avenue, with a gymnasium, bowling alleys and a hall for singing societies.

places.name: Carl Schurz Park
places.summary: A small riverside park at East 86th Street with a promenade over the East River and old Gracie Mansion in its grounds.

places.name: Third Avenue Konditorei
places.summary: A German pastry shop and coffee house under the El, with strudel, Linzer tortes, Kaffee mit Schlag and newspapers in German.

places.name: East 86th Street German and Hungarian restaurants
places.summary: Wood-paneled restaurants serving sauerbraten, goulash, schnitzel and dumplings, with near beer on the menu and something stronger for regulars.

places.name: New York Public Library
places.summary: The marble library on Fifth Avenue at 42nd Street, guarded by its stone lions, with the great Reading Room upstairs open to anyone.

places.name: Grand Central Terminal
places.summary: The New York Central's great terminal on 42nd Street, with its starry ceiling, the information booth clock and crowds of commuters.

places.name: Grand Central Oyster Bar
places.summary: The tiled vaults below the terminal, serving oyster stew and pan roasts at the counter to commuters.

places.name: Algonquin Hotel
places.summary: The hotel on West 44th Street where Dorothy Parker, Robert Benchley, Alexander Woollcott and the Round Table trade wisecracks over lunch, and where the new magazine The New Yorker was hatched.

places.name: St. Patrick's Cathedral
places.summary: The Gothic Catholic cathedral on Fifth Avenue at 50th Street, the spiritual home of Irish New York.

places.name: Saks Fifth Avenue
places.summary: The new department store at Fifth Avenue and 50th Street, opened in September 1924, for the smart set's clothes.

places.name: Tony Soma's
places.summary: Tony Soma's speakeasy in a brownstone on West 49th Street, where the Algonquin crowd drinks and the host sings opera standing on his head.

places.name: Schrafft's
places.summary: A genteel lunchroom with waitresses in black, chicken salad, ice cream sundaes and no liquor, where women shoppers lunch alone without a second glance.

places.name: Times Square
places.summary: The crossroads of Broadway and Seventh Avenue under the Times Tower, blazing with electric signs at night, with the news running in lights and crowds at every hour.

places.name: New Amsterdam Theatre
places.summary: The Art Nouveau theater on 42nd Street, home of Florenz Ziegfeld's Follies with their staircases of showgirls, comics like W. C. Fields and Will Rogers, and the Midnight Frolic on the roof.

places.name: The Palace
places.summary: The Keith-Albee vaudeville house on Broadway at 47th Street: two shows a day, and every act in America dreams of playing it.

places.name: Capitol Theatre
places.summary: The biggest movie palace in the world on Broadway at 51st Street, with over five thousand seats, a symphony orchestra, a ballet and a feature film.

places.name: Roseland Ballroom
places.summary: The dance palace on Broadway at 51st Street, where hostesses dance with customers at ten cents a dance and Fletcher Henderson's orchestra, with a young cornetist named Louis Armstrong, plays for white dancers.

places.name: Horn and Hardart Automat
places.summary: The automat on Broadway at 46th Street: walls of little glass doors, nickels from the cashier, coffee from dolphin-head spouts and pie, beans or macaroni at any hour.

places.name: Lindy's
places.summary: Leo Lindemann's delicatessen restaurant on Broadway near 50th Street, where gamblers, song writers and actors eat cheesecake after the show.

places.name: Texas Guinan's club
places.summary: Texas Guinan's speakeasy nightclub in the West Forties, greeting every customer with "Hello, suckers!", padlocked by Prohibition agents now and then and reopened under a new name.

places.name: Macy's
places.summary: The world's largest store, at Herald Square on 34th Street, newly enlarged, with bargains on every floor and crowds at Christmas.

places.name: Gimbels
places.summary: Macy's rival across Herald Square, linked by a tunnel to Pennsylvania Station, with its own bargain basement.

places.name: Pennsylvania Station
places.summary: The Pennsylvania Railroad's pink granite station modeled on the Baths of Caracalla, with a vast waiting room and glass-roofed concourse, red caps and Pullman porters.

places.name: Tin Pan Alley
places.summary: West 28th Street between Broadway and Sixth Avenue, where song publishers got their start and pianos still clatter from open windows, though the bigger firms have moved up toward Times Square.

places.name: Seventh Avenue garment lofts
places.summary: Tall new loft buildings on Seventh Avenue in the Thirties full of cutting tables and sewing machines, with racks of dresses pushed through the streets.

places.name: Keens Chop House
places.summary: The old chophouse on West 36th Street with clay pipes on the ceiling and huge mutton chops, now open to women as well as men.

places.name: Seventh Avenue cafeteria
places.summary: A big self-service cafeteria where garment workers line up at noon for soup, a sandwich and coffee, and cutters argue union politics over the tables.

places.name: Madison Square Garden
places.summary: Tex Rickard's new Garden on Eighth Avenue at 49th Street, opened at the end of November 1925, for boxing, hockey, the circus and six-day bicycle races.

places.name: West Side freight line
places.summary: Freight trains running down the middle of Tenth and Eleventh Avenues, led by a "West Side cowboy" on horseback waving a red flag; locals call it Death Avenue.

places.name: Paddy's Market
places.summary: Pushcarts and stalls under the Ninth Avenue El in the high Thirties and Forties selling fruit, fish, meat and Greek and Italian groceries, busiest on Saturday nights.

places.name: Holy Cross Church
places.summary: The Catholic church on West 42nd Street whose pastor is Father Francis Duffy, chaplain of the Fighting 69th in the war.

places.name: Stillman's Gym
places.summary: A grimy upstairs boxing gym on Eighth Avenue where fighters spar for watching managers and the public pays to look on.

places.name: Tenth Avenue speakeasy
places.summary: An old Irish saloon carrying on as a speakeasy behind soaped windows, with a peephole in the door and whiskey of doubtful origin.

places.name: Chelsea Piers
places.summary: The long granite-faced piers on the Hudson where the great Cunard and White Star liners dock, with crowds seeing passengers off to Europe.

places.name: Hotel Chelsea
places.summary: The red-brick hotel on West 23rd Street with iron balconies, long a home for writers, painters and actors who stay for years.

places.name: Old Homestead
places.summary: The steakhouse on Ninth Avenue by the meat market, serving beef since the 1860s.

places.name: Gansevoort meat market
places.summary: The wholesale meat and produce market around Gansevoort Street, loud with wagons and trucks before dawn.

places.name: Tenth Avenue lunch wagon
places.summary: An old horse-car turned diner by the piers, open all night for longshoremen, cabbies and anyone off a late ship.

places.name: Eighth Avenue speakeasy
places.summary: A cellar speakeasy on Eighth Avenue where a doorman looks you over through a slot and gin comes in coffee cups.

places.name: Washington Square Park
places.summary: The square under the marble arch at the foot of Fifth Avenue, with NYU on one side, old red-brick houses on the other and Village characters on the benches.

places.name: Chumley's
places.summary: Lee Chumley's speakeasy behind an unmarked door on Bedford Street, with a back way out through a courtyard, book jackets on the walls and writers at the tables.

places.name: Provincetown Playhouse
places.summary: The little theater on MacDougal Street where the Provincetown Players put on Eugene O'Neill's plays first.

places.name: Cherry Lane Theatre
places.summary: A little theater in an old box factory on Commerce Street, founded in 1924 by Edna St. Vincent Millay and friends.

places.name: Jack and Charlie's
places.summary: Jack Kriendler and Charlie Berns's little speakeasy in the Village, started as the Red Head in 1922 and moved and renamed since, popular with college men and newspapermen.

places.name: Romany Marie's
places.summary: Marie Marchand's candle-lit tea room, where painters, poets and inventors talk half the night over Romanian food and Turkish coffee.

places.name: Café of the Hotel Brevoort
places.summary: The French basement café of the old Brevoort on Fifth Avenue, for long lunches among writers, painters and radicals.

places.name: Union Square
places.summary: The square at 14th Street where soapbox socialists, communists and preachers argue with passers-by, and May Day rallies fill the plaza.

places.name: Flatiron Building
places.summary: The thin wedge of a skyscraper at 23rd Street, where the wind whips round the corner and lifts skirts and hats.

places.name: Lüchow's
places.summary: The big German restaurant on 14th Street, with dark wood, a string orchestra, venison and pancakes, and beer that has to be the legal kind now.

places.name: McSorley's Old Ale House
places.summary: The sawdust-floored saloon on East 7th Street near Cooper Union, men only, still pouring its own "near beer" brewed in the cellar.

places.name: Pete's Tavern
places.summary: An old Irving Place saloon carrying on behind the front of a flower shop, with booths and a long bar.

places.name: Tammany Hall
places.summary: The Democratic machine's headquarters on 14th Street, where ward bosses trade jobs and favors for votes.

places.name: Great Hall of Cooper Union
places.summary: The basement lecture hall at Astor Place where Lincoln spoke, now holding free evening lectures and debates.

places.name: Katz's Delicatessen
places.summary: The delicatessen on Houston Street at Ludlow, with hand-carved pastrami and corned beef at long counters.

places.name: Eldridge Street Synagogue
places.summary: The great Orthodox synagogue of 1887 with its rose window, its congregation thinning as families move to Brooklyn and the Bronx.

places.name: Orchard Street pushcarts
places.summary: Pushcarts lining Orchard and Hester Streets with everything from pickles to petticoats, haggled over in Yiddish.

places.name: Second Avenue Yiddish theaters
places.summary: The Yiddish Rialto on Second Avenue, with melodramas, operettas and Shakespeare in Yiddish, and stars mobbed at the stage door.

places.name: Café Royal
places.summary: The café at Second Avenue and 12th Street where Yiddish actors, writers and critics hold court over glasses of tea.

places.name: Russ's appetizing store
places.summary: Joel Russ's appetizing store on Houston Street, with smoked salmon, herring, sable and cream cheese.

places.name: Yonah Schimmel Knish Bakery
places.summary: The knish bakery on Houston Street, selling potato and kasha knishes hot from the oven.

places.name: Henry Street Settlement
places.summary: Lillian Wald's settlement house, sending visiting nurses into the tenements and running classes, clubs and a little playhouse.

places.name: Tenth Street Russian and Turkish Baths
places.summary: The steam baths on East 10th Street, with a hot rock room, cold plunge and platza scrubs.

places.name: Mulberry Street
places.summary: The crowded heart of Little Italy, with pushcarts of vegetables and clams, salumerias, and lights strung for the summer feasts.

places.name: Ferrara
places.summary: The pastry shop and café on Grand Street for espresso, cannoli and spumoni since 1892.

places.name: Lombardi's
places.summary: Gennaro Lombardi's grocery on Spring Street selling tomato pies baked in a coal oven, wrapped in paper for workers to take away.

places.name: Old St. Patrick's Cathedral
places.summary: The old cathedral on Mott Street, Irish once and now Italian, with catacombs under its walled churchyard.

places.name: Mulberry Street social club
places.summary: A storefront club for men from one village in Campania, with espresso, cards and a picture of the patron saint, members only and visitors by invitation.

places.name: Mulberry Street wine cellar
places.summary: A basement where homemade red wine is poured from barrels into jugs and glasses, quietly, for neighbors.

places.name: Doyers Street
places.summary: The crooked little street called the Bloody Angle, quiet by day and tense when the tong war between the Hip Sing and On Leong flares up, as it did again in 1924 and 1925.

places.name: Nom Wah Tea Parlor
places.summary: A bakery and tea parlor at 11 Doyers Street, opened in 1920, selling almond cookies, mooncakes and tea.

places.name: Mott Street chop suey house
places.summary: An upstairs restaurant with lanterns and carved screens serving chop suey and chow mein to sightseers and real Cantonese cooking to those who ask.

places.name: Bowery Mission
places.summary: The mission at 227 Bowery offering soup, a bed and a sermon to the men of the flophouses.

places.name: Columbus Park
places.summary: The park made where the Mulberry Bend slum of the Five Points once stood, with old men playing cards and children everywhere.

places.name: Bowery coffee-and stand
places.summary: A counter under the El at Chatham Square serving "coffee and", a mug of coffee and a doughnut, for a nickel to anyone, any hour.

places.name: City Hall and its park
places.summary: The elegant old City Hall in its park, where Mayor Hylan is serving out his term while the dapper Jimmy Walker campaigns to replace him.

places.name: Woolworth Building
places.summary: The Gothic "Cathedral of Commerce" on Broadway, tallest building in the world, with an observation deck near the top for fifty cents.

places.name: Brooklyn Bridge
places.summary: The great stone and cable bridge with a wooden promenade above the traffic, the best free walk and view in the city.

places.name: Newspaper Row
places.summary: Park Row, where the World's gold dome and the other papers' buildings face City Hall, and crowds watch bulletins posted in the windows.

places.name: Park Row lunchroom
places.summary: A narrow lunch counter where reporters, printers and court clerks eat beef stew and pie at speed.

places.name: Chambers Street speakeasy
places.summary: A speakeasy near the courts where politicians, lawyers and reporters drink together and nobody remembers anything.

places.name: New York Stock Exchange
places.summary: The temple-fronted exchange on Broad Street, roaring with a bull market, across from J. P. Morgan's offices still scarred by the 1920 bomb.

places.name: Trinity Church
places.summary: The Gothic church at the head of Wall Street, its churchyard holding Alexander Hamilton and lunching clerks.

places.name: Fraunces Tavern
places.summary: The restored colonial tavern on Pearl Street where Washington said farewell to his officers, with a museum upstairs.

places.name: Battery Park
places.summary: The harborside park at the tip of Manhattan with views of the Statue and the ships coming in.

places.name: New York Aquarium
places.summary: The free aquarium in the old round fort of Castle Clinton at the Battery, with seals, sea turtles and tanks of fish.

places.name: Ellis Island
places.summary: The immigration station in the harbor, much quieter since the quota law of 1924, where families still wait to meet relatives off the ferry.

places.name: Statue of Liberty
places.summary: The statue on Bedloe's Island, reached by ferry from the Battery, with a long climb to the crown.

places.name: Fulton Fish Market
places.summary: The wholesale fish market on South Street, busy from before dawn, with sailing ships and steamers at the old piers.

places.name: Sweet's
places.summary: The old seafood house upstairs on Fulton Street by the fish market, with broiled fish, chowder and no reservations.

places.name: Columbia Heights and Pierrepont Street
places.summary: Brownstone and Greek Revival streets on the bluff, with views of the harbor and the Manhattan skyline from the ends of the streets.

places.name: Plymouth Church
places.summary: Henry Ward Beecher's old Congregational church on Orange Street, once a stop on the Underground Railroad.

places.name: Brooklyn Academy of Music
places.summary: The grand hall on Lafayette Avenue for concerts, opera nights and lectures.

places.name: Abraham and Straus
places.summary: Brooklyn's great department store on Fulton Street.

places.name: Gage and Tollner
places.summary: The gaslit oyster and chop house on Fulton Street, with mirrored walls and waiters in long white aprons.

places.name: Fulton Street speakeasy
places.summary: A former saloon off Fulton Street pouring bootleg rye behind a cigar-store front.

places.name: Peter Luger
places.summary: The German steak house under the Williamsburg Bridge, with bare tables, porterhouse for two and waiters who have seen everything.

places.name: Williamsburg Bridge
places.summary: The steel bridge to the Lower East Side, with trolleys, the El and a footpath crossed by thousands moving to Brooklyn.

places.name: St. Stanislaus Kostka Church
places.summary: The Polish Catholic church of Greenpoint, its masses and feasts in Polish.

places.name: Manhattan Avenue shops
places.summary: Greenpoint's main street of Polish butchers, bakeries, dry goods and shoe stores.

places.name: Greenpoint Polish bakery
places.summary: A Polish bakery selling rye bread, babka and paczki, with coffee at a little counter.

places.name: Kent Avenue waterfront speakeasy
places.summary: A plain room by the refineries where sugar workers and longshoremen drink whiskey that came in by boat.

places.name: Ebbets Field
places.summary: The Brooklyn Robins' brick ballpark on Bedford Avenue, small enough that the fans in the bleachers can shout at the players.

places.name: Prospect Park
places.summary: Olmsted and Vaux's Brooklyn park with the Long Meadow, a lake for boating and skating, a carousel and a bandstand.

places.name: Brooklyn Botanic Garden
places.summary: Gardens beside Prospect Park, with a Japanese hill-and-pond garden and cherry trees in spring.

places.name: Brooklyn Museum
places.summary: The Brooklyn Institute's great museum on Eastern Parkway, with Egyptian antiquities and American paintings.

places.name: Flatbush Avenue ice cream parlor
places.summary: An ice cream parlor with wire chairs and a soda fountain, full of couples after the pictures.

places.name: Flatbush delicatessen
places.summary: A neighborhood delicatessen near the Brighton line for hot pastrami and potato salad.

places.name: Luna Park
places.summary: The fairyland of towers and minarets lit by a quarter of a million electric bulbs, with rides, shows and a ballroom.

places.name: Steeplechase Park
places.summary: George Tilyou's park under the grinning Funny Face, with mechanical horses racing round the track, the Blowhole that lifts hats and skirts, and the Pavilion of Fun.

places.name: Wonder Wheel
places.summary: The big Ferris wheel, opened in 1920, with cars that slide on rails and give riders a scare.

places.name: Nathan's
places.summary: Nathan Handwerker's stand at Surf and Stillwell selling frankfurters for a nickel since 1916, half the price of his old employer Feltman's.

places.name: Feltman's
places.summary: Charles Feltman's huge restaurant and garden on Surf Avenue, with shore dinners, a carousel and orchestras.

places.name: The Riegelmann Boardwalk
places.summary: The new boardwalk, opened in 1923, running along the beach from Coney Island toward Brighton, crowded on summer evenings.

places.name: Coney Island beach
places.summary: The packed sands where a million people come on a hot Sunday, in wool bathing suits, with lifeguards and lost-children stations.

places.name: Yankee Stadium
places.summary: The House That Ruth Built, opened in 1923 at 161st Street, with Babe Ruth in right field and a young Lou Gehrig taking over first base in 1925.

places.name: Bronx Zoo
places.summary: The New York Zoological Park in Bronx Park, with buffalo, elephants, a lion house and the bird house.

places.name: New York Botanical Garden
places.summary: Hemlock forest, gorges and the great glass conservatory beside the Bronx River.

places.name: Poe Cottage
places.summary: The little farmhouse at Fordham where Edgar Allan Poe lived in the 1840s, kept as a museum in a park on the Grand Concourse.

places.name: Arthur Avenue
places.summary: Italian Belmont's market street of pushcarts, bakeries, pork stores and cheese shops near Fordham.

places.name: Mario's
places.summary: A family restaurant on Arthur Avenue, opened in 1919, serving Neapolitan cooking.

places.name: Concourse Plaza Hotel
places.summary: The new hotel on the Concourse at 161st Street, opened in 1923, with a dining room and ballroom for Bronx weddings and ballplayers.

places.name: Famous Players-Lasky studio
places.summary: Paramount's big movie studio in Astoria, opened in 1920, where stars like Gloria Swanson make pictures near Broadway's stage actors; fans wait at the gate.

places.name: Astoria Park
places.summary: A riverside park under the arch of the Hell Gate railroad bridge, with views of the East River and Randall's Island.

places.name: Bohemian Hall
places.summary: The Czech and Slovak hall and garden on 24th Avenue, serving near beer, sausages and dumplings under the trees, and something stronger to members.

places.name: Astoria Italian bakery
places.summary: An Italian bakery and café with bread, biscotti and espresso for workers on their way to the factories.

places.name: Steinway Street German delicatessen
places.summary: A German delicatessen and lunchroom with liverwurst sandwiches, potato salad and hot dishes.

places.name: Lackawanna Terminal
places.summary: The copper-clad railroad and ferry terminal on the river, where commuters switch from trains to boats for Manhattan.

places.name: Hoboken piers
places.summary: Transatlantic piers along River Street where the Holland America liners dock and longshoremen shape up each morning.

places.name: Clam Broth House
places.summary: The waterfront clam house near the ferry with free clam broth, steamers and a long bar, long a men's haunt but serving everyone in its dining room.

places.name: Washington Street
places.summary: Hoboken's main street of bakeries, shoe stores and dry goods, a short walk from the ferry.

places.name: Elysian Park
places.summary: A small park on the cliff above the river with a view straight across to Manhattan, near where baseball was played in its early days.

places.name: River Street saloon
places.summary: One of the riverfront saloons that carry on openly enough to make Hoboken famous among thirsty New Yorkers who come over on the ferry.

careers.name: Numbers runner
careers.summary: Taking pennies, nickels and dimes on the day's three-digit number from tenement to barbershop and carrying the slips to the bank before the number comes out.

careers.name: Song plugger
careers.summary: Playing and singing a music publisher's new songs for bandleaders, vaudevillians and dime-store customers to get them heard.

careers.name: Skyscraper riveter
careers.summary: Working in a four-person riveting gang on the steel of the new towers: heating, tossing, catching and driving red-hot rivets hundreds of feet up.

careers.name: Shoeshine
careers.summary: Shining shoes at a stand in a station, a hotel lobby or on a street corner, a nickel or a dime a shine and tips.

careers.name: Cigarette seller
careers.summary: Walking a nightclub with a tray of cigarettes, cigars and candy on a strap, selling to the tables and living on tips.

careers.name: Pushcart peddler
careers.summary: Renting a pushcart and a license to sell fruit, fish, notions or clothing on a market street, haggling from dawn till dark.

careers.name: Taxi dancer
careers.summary: Dancing with paying customers at ten cents a dance in a ballroom, earning a share of every ticket.

careers.name: Subway guard
careers.summary: Riding the subway or El between cars, opening and closing the gates and calling the stations.

careers.name: Elevator operator
careers.summary: Running an elevator in an office tower, hotel or department store in a uniform and white gloves, calling the floors.

employers.name: New York Stock Exchange
employers.summary: The exchange on Broad Street and the brokerage houses around it, busy with a rising market.

employers.name: J. P. Morgan and Company
employers.summary: The private bank at 23 Wall Street, the most powerful in the country.

employers.name: New York Telephone Company
employers.summary: The telephone company, with exchanges all over the city full of operators at switchboards.

employers.name: The New York World
employers.summary: Pulitzer's crusading paper under the gold dome on Park Row.

employers.name: The New Yorker
employers.summary: Harold Ross's new weekly magazine on West 45th Street, first published in February 1925.

employers.name: The Jewish Daily Forward
employers.summary: The Yiddish daily in its tall building on East Broadway, read by hundreds of thousands.

employers.name: R. H. Macy and Company
employers.summary: The world's largest store at Herald Square.

employers.name: Ziegfeld Follies, New Amsterdam Theatre
employers.summary: Florenz Ziegfeld's revue on 42nd Street.

employers.name: The Cotton Club
employers.summary: The Harlem nightclub at Lenox Avenue and 142nd Street, run by Owney Madden's people.

employers.name: Roseland Ballroom
employers.summary: The Broadway dance palace with ten-cents-a-dance hostesses and big bands.

employers.name: Shapiro, Bernstein and Company
employers.summary: A Tin Pan Alley music publisher whose pluggers push its songs all over town.

employers.name: Pennsylvania Railroad at Pennsylvania Station
employers.summary: The railroad and its Pullman sleeping cars, with porters, red caps, clerks and a shoeshine stand in the station.

employers.name: Interborough Rapid Transit Company
employers.summary: The company running the IRT subway and the Manhattan Els, with its great powerhouse on the West Side.

employers.name: New York Police Department
employers.summary: The police, from headquarters on Centre Street to the precinct houses.

employers.name: Bellevue Hospital
employers.summary: The great city hospital on First Avenue, taking anyone who comes through the door.

employers.name: Harlem Hospital
employers.summary: The city hospital on Lenox Avenue, where Black doctors and nurses have only lately won places on the staff.

employers.name: Brooklyn Navy Yard
employers.summary: The Navy's shipyard, building and refitting warships.

employers.name: American Sugar Refining Company
employers.summary: The big Williamsburg refinery on the East River, makers of Domino sugar.

employers.name: Famous Players-Lasky Corporation, Astoria
employers.summary: Paramount's movie studio in Astoria.

employers.name: Cunard Line, Chelsea Piers
employers.summary: The British line whose liners dock at the Chelsea piers, hiring longshoremen by the shape-up.

career_hubs.name: Wall Street and Park Row
career_hubs.summary: Banks, brokers, insurance, the telephone and telegraph companies, newspapers and City Hall.

career_hubs.name: Broadway and Midtown
career_hubs.summary: Theaters, hotels, restaurants, department stores, the two great stations, publishers, and the building sites of the new towers.

career_hubs.name: Harlem
career_hubs.summary: Cabarets, churches, hospitals, shops and the numbers banks of Black New York.

career_hubs.name: The garment trades
career_hubs.summary: Cloak, suit and dress shops on Seventh Avenue and the workshops, pushcarts and settlement houses of the Lower East Side.

career_hubs.name: The waterfront and the works
career_hubs.summary: Piers, freight yards, refineries, bakeries, piano works and the Navy Yard on both rivers.

climate.summary: Four sharp seasons: cold, gray winters with snow and slush, humid summers so hot that people sleep on fire escapes, roofs and the beach, and fine clear springs and autumns.

months.note: Cold; snow piles up in the gutters and coal stoves burn all day.
Raw and slushy; skating in Central Park when the ponds freeze.
Windy; St. Patrick's Day parade on Fifth Avenue.
Showers; the baseball season opens and Easter bonnets parade.
Mild and green; straw boaters come out on the fifteenth.
Warm; Coney Island opens for the season.
Hot and sticky; tenement families sleep on roofs and fire escapes.
Heat waves and thunderstorms; the beaches are packed.
Warm and clear; felt hats replace straw on the fifteenth.
Crisp and bright, the best month in the city.
Gray and chilly; football and the Thanksgiving parade.
Cold; store windows dressed for Christmas and the first snow.

annual_events.name: New Year's Eve in Times Square
annual_events.summary: Crowds pack Times Square to watch the lighted ball drop down the flagpole of the Times Tower at midnight, and the speakeasies and hotels are booked solid.

annual_events.name: St. Patrick's Day Parade
annual_events.summary: Irish New York marches up Fifth Avenue past St. Patrick's Cathedral with bands, county societies and the Fighting 69th.

annual_events.name: Easter Parade on Fifth Avenue
annual_events.summary: After Easter services New Yorkers stroll up Fifth Avenue in new hats and spring clothes to see and be seen.

annual_events.name: Baseball season
annual_events.summary: The Giants at the Polo Grounds, the Yankees at their new stadium in the Bronx and the Robins at Ebbets Field, with the scores chalked up in barbershops all over town.

annual_events.name: World Series bulletin boards
annual_events.summary: Crowds fill Times Square and Park Row to follow the World Series play by play on giant electric scoreboards outside the newspapers.

annual_events.name: Fourth of July
annual_events.summary: Firecrackers in every street, fireworks over the harbor and a record crowd at Coney Island.

annual_events.name: Coney Island Mardi Gras
annual_events.summary: A week of parades, floats, costumes and confetti on Surf Avenue to close the summer season.

annual_events.name: The High Holy Days
annual_events.summary: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur close the shops of the Lower East Side, fill the synagogues and send families to the river for tashlikh.

annual_events.name: Armistice Day
annual_events.summary: Veterans parade on Fifth Avenue and the city falls silent at eleven o'clock on the eleventh.

annual_events.name: Macy's Thanksgiving Parade
annual_events.summary: Macy's parade, first held in 1924, with employees in costume, floats, bands and animals borrowed from the Central Park Menagerie, ending at the store's Christmas windows.

annual_events.name: Six-day bicycle race
annual_events.summary: Riders circle the board track at Madison Square Garden day and night for six days, and society comes late to watch the sprints.

annual_events.name: Chinese New Year
annual_events.summary: Firecrackers, lion dances and banquets on Mott and Pell Streets to welcome the new year.

local_color.name: The bee's knees
local_color.summary: Anything excellent is "the bee's knees" or "the cat's pajamas", a good time is "the berries" and a fine fellow is "the real McCoy".

local_color.name: Hooch, giggle water and the blind pig
local_color.summary: Liquor is "hooch", "giggle water" or "bathtub gin"; a speakeasy is a "speak" or a "blind pig", and a raid means the place has been "padlocked".

local_color.name: The big apple
local_color.summary: Horse-racing people, following the Morning Telegraph's turf writer, call the big New York races "the big apple", the prize every stable is after.

local_color.name: Applesauce and banana oil
local_color.summary: Nonsense is "applesauce" or "banana oil", money is "dough" or "kale", and a person who can't keep a secret "spills the beans".

local_color.name: The password at the door
local_color.summary: You knock, a slot opens in the door and you say who sent you or the password of the week; the doorman decides.

local_color.name: Rent parties
local_color.summary: Harlem tenants throw Saturday-night parties with a piano player, fried chicken and a jug, charging a quarter at the door to make the rent; cards in the elevators announce them.

local_color.name: The Seventh Avenue stroll
local_color.summary: After church on Sunday Harlem promenades up Seventh Avenue in its best clothes, stopping to talk and show off.

local_color.name: Playing the numbers
local_color.summary: Pennies on a three-digit number taken from the day's bank clearings, with dream books to turn a dream into a number; runners collect from barbershops and stoops.

local_color.name: The Charleston
local_color.summary: The dance from the Broadway show Runnin' Wild that everyone, flappers above all, is doing in 1925, kicking up their heels.

local_color.name: The automat
local_color.summary: Get a handful of nickels from the woman in the glass booth, then drop them in the slot beside the little window for a slice of pie or a plate of beans.

local_color.name: A Nathan's frankfurter
local_color.summary: A grilled frankfurter on a roll with mustard, a nickel at Nathan's, eaten on the street with a glass of root beer.

local_color.name: Pastrami on rye
local_color.summary: Hand-sliced hot pastrami piled on rye bread with mustard and a pickle, from the delicatessens of the Lower East Side.

local_color.name: Egg cream
local_color.summary: Chocolate syrup, milk and a shot of seltzer whipped to a foam in a glass, with no egg and no cream, from any candy store fountain.

local_color.name: Cheesecake
local_color.summary: Rich cream-cheese cheesecake, which Broadway eats after the show and argues about.

local_color.name: Bathtub gin and needle beer
local_color.summary: Alcohol cut with water and juniper oil in a tub, and near beer "needled" with alcohol, are what most speakeasies pour; good Scotch comes from rum row off the coast and costs plenty.

local_color.name: Knishes
local_color.summary: Potato or kasha baked in a thin crust, hot from the pushcart or the bakery for a few cents.

local_color.name: Chop suey
local_color.summary: Chop suey and chow mein at Chinatown and uptown chop suey houses, the city's cheap late-night meal.

local_color.name: The Giants
local_color.summary: John McGraw's New York Giants of the National League at the Polo Grounds, National League champions four years running from 1921 to 1924.

local_color.name: The Yankees
local_color.summary: The Yankees of Babe Ruth at their new stadium in the Bronx; in 1925 the Babe is sick for much of the season and a young Lou Gehrig takes first base.

local_color.name: The Brooklyn Robins
local_color.summary: Brooklyn's National League club, called the Robins after manager Wilbert Robinson, or the Dodgers after the trolley dodgers who follow them.

local_color.name: Pushcart markets
local_color.summary: Pushcarts line Orchard, Hester, Mulberry and Bleecker Streets, Arthur Avenue and the Ninth Avenue market, selling anything at prices that start a haggle.

local_color.name: Sleeping on the fire escape
local_color.summary: In a heat wave tenement families carry mattresses onto roofs and fire escapes and children sleep in the parks.

local_color.name: Straw Hat Day
local_color.summary: Men switch to straw boaters on May 15 and back to felt on September 15; a straw hat worn after that is fair game to be knocked off and smashed in the street.

at a lunch counter or automat

balcony to orchestra; the Follies more
a ride across Midtown, plus tip
